In [[mathematics]], the '''Whitney inequality''' gives an upper bound for the error of best approximation of a function by [[polynomial]]s in terms of the [[modulus of smoothness|moduli of smoothness]]. It was first proved by [[Hassler Whitney]] in 1957,<ref name=Whitneypaper>{{cite journal|last1=Hassler|first1=Whitney|title=On Functions with Bounded nth Differences|journal=J. Math. Pures Appl.|date=1957|volume=36|issue=IX|pages=67–95}}<br/>{{cite book |author-mask=1 |last=Whitney |first=H. |chapter=On functions with bounded nth differences |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4612-2972-8_28 |editor-last=Eells |editor-first=J. |editor2-last=Toledo |editor2-first=D. |title=Hassler Whitney Collected Papers |publisher=Birkhäuser Boston |series=Contemporary Mathematicians |date=1992 |isbn=978-1-4612-2972-8 |pages=407–435 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-2972-8_28}}</ref> and is an important tool in the field of [[approximation theory]] for obtaining upper estimates on the errors of best approximation.

==Statement of the theorem==

Denote the value of the best uniform approximation of a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f\in C([a,b])</math> by algebraic [[polynomials]] <math>P_n</math> of degree <math>\leq n</math> by

: <math> E_n(f)_{[a,b]} := \inf_{P_n}{\| f-P_n \|_{C([a,b])}} </math>

The [[modulus of smoothness|moduli of smoothness]] of order <math>k</math> of a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f\in C([a,b])</math> are defined as:

: <math>\omega_k(t):=\omega_k(t;f;[a,b]) :=\sup_{h\in [0,t]} \|\Delta_h^k(f;\cdot)\|_{C([a,b-kh])} \quad \text{ for } \quad t\in [0,(b-a)/k],</math>

: <math>\omega_k(t):=\omega_k((b-a)/k)\quad \text{ for} \quad t>(b-a)/k ,</math>

where <math>\Delta_h^k</math> is the [[finite difference]] of order <math>k</math>.

'''Theorem:''' <ref name=UnifApprox>{{cite book|last1=Dzyadyk|first1=Vladislav K.|last2=Shevchuk|first2=Igor A.|title=Theory of Uniform Approximation of Functions by Polynomials|year=2008 |publisher=de Gruyter |isbn=978-3-11-020147-5 |chapter=3. On smoothness of functions §3.6 |chapter-url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110208245.167/html |doi=10.1515/9783110208245.167 |pages=231–3 |oclc=560639251}}</ref> [Whitney, 1957] If <math>f\in C([a,b])</math>, then

: <math>E_{k-1}(f)_{[a,b]}\leq W_k \omega_k\left(\frac{b-a}{k};f;[a,b]\right) </math>

where <math>W_k</math> is a constant depending only on <math>k</math>. The Whitney constant <math>W(k)</math> is the smallest value of <math>W_k</math> for which the above inequality holds. The theorem is particularly useful when applied on intervals of small length, leading to good estimates on the error of [[spline (mathematics)|spline]] approximation.

==Proof==
The original proof given by Whitney follows an analytic argument which utilizes the properties of [[modulus of smoothness|moduli of smoothness]]. However, it can also be proved in a much shorter way using Peetre's K-functionals.<ref name=DeLo>{{cite book|last1=Devore|first1=R.A.K.|last2=Lorentz|first2=G.G.|title=Constructive Approximation |publisher=Springer |chapter=6. ''K''-Functionals and Interpolation Spaces §4 Two Theorems of Whitney: Theorem 4.2 |chapter-url={{GBurl|cDqNW6k7_ZwC|p=183}} |pages=183– |series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften |volume=303 |isbn=978-3-642-08075-3 |oclc=1058163028 |orig-year=1993 |year=2010}}</ref>

Let:

: <math>x_0:=a, \quad h:=\frac{b-a}{k}, \quad x_j:=x+0+jh, \quad F(x) = \int_a^x f(u) \, du,</math>

: <math>G(x):=F(x)-L(x;F;x_0,\ldots,x_k), \quad g(x):=G'(x),</math>

: <math>\omega_k(t):=\omega_k(t;f;[a,b])\equiv \omega_k(t;g;[a,b])</math>

where <math>L(x;F;x_0,\ldots,x_k)</math> is the [[Lagrange polynomial]] for <math>F</math> at the nodes <math>\{x_0,\ldots,x_k\}</math>.

Now fix some <math>x\in [a,b]</math> and choose <math>\delta</math> for which <math>(x+k\delta)\in [a,b]</math>. Then:

: <math>\int_0^1 \Delta_{t\delta}^k (g;x) \, dt =(-1)^kg(x)+\sum_{j=1}^k (-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j} \int_0^1 g(x+jt\delta) \, dt</math>

: <math>=(-1)^kg(x)+\sum_{j=1}^k{(-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j} \frac{1}{j\delta}(G(x+j\delta)-G(x))}, </math>

Therefore:

: <math>|g(x)| \leq \int_0^1 |\Delta_{t\delta}^k(g;x)| \, dt + \frac{2}{|\delta|}\|G\|_{C([a,b])} \sum_{j=1}^k \binom{k}{j}\frac{1}{j} \leq \omega_k(|\delta|)+\frac{1}{|\delta|}2^{k+1}\|G\|_{C([a,b])} </math>

And since we have <math>\|G\|_{C([a,b])}\leq h\omega_k(h)</math>, (a property of [[modulus of smoothness|moduli of smoothness]])

: <math>E_{k-1}(f)_{[a,b]}\leq \|g\|_{C([a,b])} \leq \omega_k(|\delta|) +\frac{1}{|\delta|} h 2^{k+1}\omega_k(h). </math> 

Since <math>\delta</math> can always be chosen in such a way that <math>h\geq |\delta| \geq h/2</math>, this completes the proof.

==Whitney constants and Sendov's conjecture==

It is important to have sharp estimates of the Whitney constants. It is easily shown that <math>W(1)=1/2</math>, and it was first proved by [[John Charles Burkill|Burkill]] (1952) that <math>W(2)\leq 1</math>, who conjectured that <math>W(k)\leq 1</math> for all <math>k</math>. [[Hassler Whitney|Whitney]] was also able to prove that <ref name=UnifApprox />

: <math>W(2)=\frac{1}{2}, \quad \frac{8}{15}\leq W(3) \leq 0.7 \quad W(4)\leq 3.3 \quad W(5)\leq 10.4</math> 

and

: <math>W(k)\geq \frac{1}{2},\quad k\in\mathbb{N} </math>

In 1964, Brudnyi was able to obtain the estimate <math>W(k)=O(k^{2k})</math>, and in 1982, Sendov proved that <math>W(k)\leq (k+1)k^k</math>.  Then, in 1985, Ivanov and Takev proved that <math>W(k)=O(k\ln k)</math>, and Binev proved that <math>W(k)=O(k)</math>. Sendov conjectured that <math>W(k)\leq 1</math> for all <math>k</math>, and in 1985 was able to prove that the Whitney constants are bounded above by an absolute constant, that is, <math>W(k)\leq 6</math> for all <math>k</math>. Kryakin, Gilewicz, and Shevchuk (2002)<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gilewicz|first1=J.|last2=Kryakin|first2=Yu. V.|last3=Shevchuk|first3=I. A.|title=Boundedness by 3 of the Whitney Interpolation Constant|journal=Journal of Approximation Theory|date=2002|volume=119|issue=2|pages=271–290|doi=10.1006/jath.2002.3732|doi-access=free}}</ref> were able to show that <math>W(k)\leq 2</math> for <math>k \leq 82000</math>, and that <math>W(k)\leq 2+\frac{1}{e^2}</math> for all <math>k</math>.
